name: Hair analysis (mineral hair testing)

card.summary: Laboratory measurement of minerals and metals in a hair sample, used by some practitioners to design supplement and detox plans aimed at healthier hair, skin and overall appearance.
card.aka: Hair tissue mineral analysis, HTMA, hair mineral analysis
card.note: Major medical bodies have stated that commercial hair mineral testing is not validated for diagnosing individuals.

quick.overview:
Hair analysis sends a small snippet of hair to a laboratory that measures its content of minerals such as calcium, magnesium, zinc and copper, and of toxic metals such as lead, mercury and arsenic. Practitioners in some branches of alternative and nutritional medicine read the resulting profile as a picture of mineral balance and toxic load.

People interested in looks use it because hair, skin and nails are often discussed as the visible face of nutrition: a report that flags a low mineral or a high metal becomes the basis for a supplement or detox plan aimed at stronger hair, clearer skin or more energy. Researchers use hair testing in population studies and in forensic and drug testing, while medical reviews have questioned its use for diagnosing an individual's mineral status.
quick.how: A person (or practitioner) snips a small sample of hair close to the scalp, mails it to a commercial laboratory, and receives a report of element levels and ratios, often with a suggested supplement list. Results are typically discussed with a nutrition or naturopathic practitioner and repeated after a few months.
quick.risks: The test itself is non-invasive. The reported concerns are about interpretation: the American Medical Association has called the use of hair analysis to decide on therapy an unproven practice, and reviews note that results can be affected by shampoos, dyes, bleaching and environmental contamination. Supplement or chelation plans built on a report carry their own risks and costs.

lead: Hair analysis is the chemical or microscopic examination of hair. In alternative and nutritional medicine, hair mineral analysis (also called hair tissue mineral analysis) measures minerals and metals in a hair sample to screen for toxic exposure, assess mineral status and guide supplement programs.[1][2] Because hair grows roughly a centimetre a month, it also holds a time-ordered record of what the body has taken in, which is why it is used in drug testing and poisoning investigations.[3][4]

In appearance-focused circles, the appeal is that hair, skin and nails are treated as outward signs of internal nutrition. A report showing, for example, low zinc or elevated copper can be used to justify a plan of supplements, dietary changes or detox protocols intended to improve hair thickness, skin clarity and general vitality. Proponents cite its low cost, non-invasiveness and ability to measure many elements at once.[1]

Research bodies describe hair analysis as well established for forensic toxicology, drug exposure and population-level studies, and as unvalidated for diagnosing an individual's nutrient status. A 1985 review in the Canadian Medical Association Journal concluded that commercial laboratory hair analysis could not yet be justified in clinical practice, and the American Medical Association has opposed its use to decide on medical therapy.[1][5][6]

chain: Hair sample is analysed for minerals and metals
Report is read as a picture of nutrient balance
Supplement or diet plan is built from it
Aim: stronger hair, clearer skin, more energy
angle.text: People send in a hair sample so a report can point to a mineral they are said to be low in or a metal they are said to carry, then use that report to choose supplements or dietary changes aimed at hair quality and skin. The chain runs through the plan the report inspires rather than through the test itself.

paras: Hair is made mainly of keratin and grows in cycles of growth, regression and rest, at an average of about 1 cm per month, so segments along the shaft correspond to successive weeks or months.[3] Substances circulating in the blood can be incorporated into the hair as it forms, which is the basis for testing it for drugs, hormones such as cortisol, and elements.[4][7]

Commercial hair mineral analysis reports typically list levels of nutrient minerals and toxic metals and sometimes ratios between them (for example calcium to magnesium). The report is usually accompanied by interpretation and a supplement or detox recommendation from the laboratory or a practitioner.[1]

sections.h: Use in appearance and wellness circles
paras: Practitioners in some branches of alternative medicine use hair analysis to screen for heavy metal exposure and to look for suspected mineral deficiencies. Advocates also use it to explain hair thinning, dull skin or low energy and to select supplements.[1]
The practice sits alongside other test-and-supplement approaches in the wellness world, in which a measurement is used to personalise a regimen.

A 1985 critical review in the Canadian Medical Association Journal described hair trace-element analysis as potentially safe, noninvasive and useful, but said it had not been proven reliable or shown to reflect trace-element status elsewhere in the body, and noted that normal ranges were poorly known.[5] A 1985 JAMA study of commercial hair analysis reached a similarly cautious conclusion about laboratories' reliability.[6]

A later review described by Wikipedia found hair metal and mineral analysis useful for large population studies, epidemiology and chronically exposed groups, but not for diagnosing an individual.[1] A paper on interpretation problems lists factors that complicate results, including external contamination and cosmetic treatment of the hair.[8]
Hair is a more established tool in other fields. Reviews describe its value for detecting drug and alcohol use over longer windows than urine, and for measuring long-term cortisol exposure.[9][10]

Reviews of commercial hair mineral analysis have concluded that it has not been shown to be reliable for diagnosing individual patients, and no trial is cited showing that supplement plans guided by hair test results improve hair or skin outcomes.[5][6] Hair testing has been studied in drug-use detection and cortisol measurement, where reviews describe it as a useful biomarker tool.[9][10]

Hair analysis in forensics has a separate history: microscopic comparison of hairs was accepted in courts by the 1950s, and DNA testing later showed that matches had been overstated. A 2015 US Justice Department review found flawed testimony in 257 of 268 examined trials, according to Wikipedia.[1] This is a different technique from mineral testing.

timeline.event: Critical reviews of commercial hair analysis published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal and JAMA.[5][6]
Review of cortisol analysis in hair published, describing the state of the art.[9]
US Justice Department review of microscopic hair comparison testimony.[1]

lore.intro: Hair mineral testing is discussed in wellness and nutrition communities as a way to personalise supplements and detox plans.

claims.claim: A hair test reveals a person's mineral deficiencies and toxic metal load
claims.believers: Proponents say hair accumulates elements over weeks to months and that a multi-element report is a low-cost, non-invasive window into nutritional status.[1]
claims.experts: Reviews state that hair analysis has not been proven to reflect trace-element status elsewhere in the body and that the AMA opposes its use to decide therapy.[1][5]

claims.claim: Hair mineral ratios can guide supplement plans that improve hair and skin
claims.believers: Practitioners who use the reports build supplement regimens around the reported levels and ratios.[1]
claims.experts: No published trial is cited showing that regimens chosen this way improve hair or skin outcomes.[5][6]
